text: The Minister of War (French: Ministre de la guerre) was the highest-ranking official in the French Ministry of War and served as a key position within the Government of France from 1791 to 1947. This role replaced the Secretary of State for War and, later, was merged with the offices of Minister of the Navy and Minister of Air to create the Minister of the Armed Forces. In 1791, during the French Revolution, the Secretary of State for War was renamed Minister of War. For the majority of its history until the early 20th century, the office was held exclusively by Marshals or Generals; however, the Third Republic gradually transitioned to civilian politicians occupying the position, though this shift was often disrupted by the governmental instability of the era, resulting in many ministers serving only for a few days. On 27 April 1791, the National Constituent Assembly passed a decree establishing the six ministries—Justice, Interior, Finances, War, Navy, and Foreign Affairs. This decree was formally enacted into law on 25 May 1791 by King Louis XVI. The law assigned the Minister of War full authority over the French Army and sole responsibility for the provost duties of the National Gendarmerie, as well as oversight of the administration and finances of the ministry.
